title: The smudged label
note: Fictional unit and patients. Your reuse program’s procedures, the nurse, and the medical director come first.
intro: You are the reprocessing technician. At 11:10 on Wednesday, a covered tray arrives from the morning shift. One dialyzer’s label has been smudged by germicide: you can read the surname “Cruz” but not the first name or the second identifier. Two patients named Cruz dialyzed this morning, Mr. Antonio Cruz (station 4) and Mrs. Elena Cruz (station 7). Both use the same dialyzer model.

n1.prompt: What do you do with it?

choices.text: Quarantine it as unidentified and report it; do not process it.
choices.feedback: A label that is unreadable or does not match the record makes the dialyzer unidentified. Never relabel from memory: a wrong guess sends one patient’s dialyzer to another.

choices.text: Relabel it as Mr. Antonio Cruz’s, since it came from the station 4 side of the tray and his session ended first.
choices.feedback: Relabeling from memory or position is exactly how wrong-patient dialyzers happen. Exposure to another person’s blood residue is a serious event.
choices.then: You stop before writing, quarantine it, and report it.

choices.text: Process it now and work out the name before it is needed.
choices.feedback: Processing an unidentified dialyzer links its record to a guess. Identity is the first gate; nothing else matters if it fails.
choices.then: You quarantine it instead and report it.

n2.scene: At 12:40 a nurse calls: “Bring Cruz’s dialyzer for the 1 p.m. shift.” A third Cruz, Mr. Ramil Cruz, dialyzes at 1 p.m.

choices.text: Ask for the full name and a second identifier, read it back, and pick by label.
choices.feedback: “Cruz’s dialyzer” fits three patients today. Full name plus a second identifier, read back, every time.

vitals.request: Mr. Ramil Cruz + ID read back

choices.text: Take the Cruz dialyzer at the front of the shelf.
choices.feedback: Picking by position is a classic trap. Same surname, same model, different patient.
choices.then: You check the label: it is Mrs. Elena Cruz’s. You call back for the full name and identifier.

vitals.request: Mr. Ramil Cruz + ID read back

choices.text: Ask “Which Cruz?” and take the dialyzer with that first name on the label, since the nurse knows her patient.
choices.feedback: Better, but add the second identifier and read it back. First names can be similar too.
choices.then: You also confirm his second identifier and read it back.

vitals.request: Mr. Ramil Cruz + ID read back

vitals.shelf: Mr. Ramil Cruz moved shifts yesterday; map not updated

n3.scene: Mr. Ramil Cruz’s dialyzer is not in his slot. You find it in the evening-shift slot: he moved from evenings to 1 p.m. yesterday, and the storage map was not updated.

choices.text: Confirm it by label and identifiers, update the map now, and move it to the right slot.
choices.feedback: Patients who change shift are a known trap. Update the map the same day; storage is by labeled slot, but identity is always by the label itself.

choices.text: Take it, and leave the map for whoever works the evening shift.
choices.feedback: An outdated map sends the next technician to the wrong slot. Fix it now.
choices.then: You update the map before leaving the room.

choices.text: Use the one in his old slot, since that was his slot until yesterday, and update the map at the end of the day.
choices.feedback: Never identify by slot. Read the label and both identifiers, then fix the map.
choices.then: You read the label: it is his. You update the map.

vitals.status: Nurse at the door, in a hurry

n4.scene: The nurse comes to the door. “I’m in a hurry; I’ll check it at the chair.”

choices.text: Read the label aloud with her against the record, and log the release.
choices.feedback: No dialyzer leaves the room without a two-person read-back. The check at the chair against the wristband is the next gate, not a replacement for this one.

choices.text: Hand it over; she will check it at the chair.
choices.feedback: Deferring the check is one of the breaks in the chain. If the chair check is rushed too, the wrong dialyzer reaches a patient.

choices.text: Hand it over with a sticky note of his full name and identifier, so she can match it to his wristband at the chair.
choices.feedback: A note is not a check. Read it aloud together and log it.

n5.scene: By 15:00 the program lead reviews the quarantined dialyzer. The use number and processing records cannot settle whose it is.
n5.prompt: What happens to it, and what changes?

choices.text: It is not used; it is discarded per procedure, and the unit moves to durable labels and name alerts.
choices.feedback: An unidentified dialyzer cannot be made safe by deduction. Prevent the next one: labels that survive germicide, name alerts, and separate storage for similar names.

choices.text: Give it to whichever Cruz has the closer use number in the records, since the use count is the best evidence available.
choices.feedback: A guess, however clever, can expose a patient to another’s blood residue. Unidentified means not used.

choices.text: Keep it in quarantine in case someone remembers.
choices.feedback: Memory is not identification. Resolve it by procedure, and fix the labels.

end.title: Next month
end.text: The unit now prints water-resistant labels at first use, flags same-surname patients with a name alert, and stores them on different shelves. The reuse log shows a two-person read-back for every release. There have been no unidentified dialyzers since.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Identity is the first gate. An unreadable label means quarantine; never relabel from memory.
  • Full name plus a second identifier, read back, for every request.
  • Never pick by shelf position; update the storage map the same day.
  • Two-person read-back before anything leaves the room.
  • Fix the system: durable labels, name alerts, separate storage.

See The label, The chain of custody and Similar names.
